paragraphs.text: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, "literature"] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as 'that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = ‘with’) the trends of lifeʼ… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, 'that which co-exists with hita [welfare]ʼ. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, ‘Art for artʼs sake,ʼ cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement ‘Art for artʼs sakeʼ is not acceptable; rather we should say, 'Art for service and blessedness.ʼ… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

paragraphs.text: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted above. But he did not stop there. Going a step further, he translated his words into actions, giving a direct example by creating his own literature, which is marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories was written in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part series was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that, in October 2010, a volume named Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume was published. Now, we are extremely happy to publish Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 4, 5, 6. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all the remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

paragraphs.text: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast range of topics from linguistics and philology to history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books.

paragraphs.text: Betel leaf connoisseurs used to regularly flock to her from far and near, from Tollah to Tollygunge, from Belgachia to Bajeshivpur crowding around her shop. She had wonderful dexterity in making betel-leaves with just the right mix of lime and catechu. Although a trifle costly, she put some real betel-nuts in her product – a hundred percent pure betel-nuts and not the adulterated stuff of chopped coconut shells. Her conduct was excellent too. She was never ingratiating but always behaved politely. She used to bring pure betel-leaves every day all the way from Bagnan, garden-fresh so to say, because stale leaves never tasted good. Every client paid her the price she asked for, except Rámt́ahal Singh, the night watchman. Rámt́ahal Singh would casually turn up at her shop at all hours, banging the baton and demand, “Hey, Put́ii, give me a betel-leaf.” Put́uráńii would then sulkily give him one. This man never paid her, as if it were his birthright to get things for free.

paragraphs.text: The higher officers said, “Rámt́ahal was carrying out his duty, but you bit him and prevented him from doing just that. Why did you obstruct him? Why?”

Everyone was curious to see the woman who had bitten a police watchman! The bailiff called out the concerned names one by one.

As long as there are hand-pulled rickshaws, by what logic can action be taken against a rickshaw puller for soiling the roads? paragraphs.text: “There is a serious allegation against you,” said the judge, “You obstructed a government employee from doing his duty. Why did you bite his wrist?”
summary: “There is a serious allegation against you,” said the judge, “You obstructed a government employee from doing his duty. Why did you bite his wrist?”

paragraphs.text: Put́uráńii said, “If a thief enters a house to steal and the householder bites his arm, would you call it ”obstructing a government servant in his duty?“ That scoundrel Rámt́ahal used to demand free betel leaves from me every day. He acted as if it were his right! On that day I found he and his party were grabbing a lot of betel-leaves and running away with fistfuls of chopped betel-nuts. I thought, this could never be rightfully his! He was doing this to me because I was a weak, uncomplaining woman; so, I bit on his wrist. Now Mr. Magistrate, you are an honourable man. Tell me what wrong did I do?”

paragraphs.text: Put́uráńii looked at the judge and continued, “Your Honour, I may be a weak woman, but I do notice whatʼs going on around me. There is a small teashop near my place. Rámt́ahal takes tea over there every day but does not pay for it. The tea-vendor is too scared to ask for money. There is also a vegetable-seller nearby. Rámt́ahal often picks up potatoes and wax gourd, slices of pumpkins and other vegetables, without paying a paisa. The vegetable-seller doesnʼt have the courage to ask him to pay.

paragraphs.text: Earlier, when I had my shop in Baidyabati, I noticed the watchman there who manned the level crossing. He would stop all the vegetable-laden trucks going to the local market by lowering the barriers and take whatever he wanted of vegetables such as potatoes, bananas, etc. Then he would profit by selling the stolen vegetables at cheaper rates in the local market. Why donʼt you visit the place personally and see if I am speaking the truth or not? Donʼt announce your plans beforehand if you decide to visit the place. Go quietly, privately, because, if the sinners get to know of your plans, they will either pretend to be saints or make themselves unavailable. Your Honour, may I take your leave now ?”

paragraphs.text: “Oh yes, another matter before I go! Today you have shown everyone how to dispense justice, my son. Let the world know and learn what actual justice is all about. But I never knew how tough the job of a judge was, my son. How trying! With pen in hand, you have to sit there all day with a thoughtful expression, resting your cheek on your palms. If you work so hard, your health may give way. Do you take some milk in the morning, or do you just gulp down some tea and biscuits and come to work? Oh, what a nice boy you are, you remind me of my grandson! If he were alive today, he would be like you. Because you feel for the poor, and thus earn virtues, my son, I would like you to remain a judge for all time to come and thus – removing the suffering of the poor in this way – even in your future births. But the job of a judge is a really trying one! If you feel it is too hard for you, you could be a lawyer or a court clerk. Even in such jobs there is enough scope to do a lot of good to the poor. But if you ask me, I would like you to continue as a judge sitting on that chair for ever and ever. And I, Put́uráńii Dásii, seller of cháṋcii betel-leaves, give you my solemn word that, in every future birth of mine, I will come personally and supply you with betel-leaves. You wouldnʼt then be able to put me off, by saying that they would stain your teeth or that the spittle would be a bother! Put́uráńii wouldnʼt be swayed by such evasive arguments of yours. You would have to chew betel-leaves prepared by me whether you liked it or not!”

paragraphs.text: As Put́uráńii came out of the court, a group of reporters surrounded her.
summary: As Put́uráńii came out of the court, a group of reporters surrounded her.

paragraphs.text: She said irritably, “Who the hell are you? Why have you cornered me so? What nonsense! Just because I am a weak and uncomplaining woman, you harass me like this ? All right, tell me what you want to know.”

paragraphs.text: “No one, actually. My husband is dead, and so are my sons. I had a grandson but he too died long ago. If he were alive today, he would be as old as the judge. My youngest daughter is the only one left in the family to call me ‘mother’, but she hasnʼt turned out to my liking. She has joined the film industry and is earning quite well, but she doesnʼt feel the distress of the poor. She never gives to charity – she thinks everyone was born with a silver spoon in their mouth, but, what does all this matter to you? Why have you cornered me like this?”

paragraphs.text: She said, “The thought of my parents just came to my mind just now. They were such good people, you know. They loved me very, very much. They loved me, each in their own different way. My father used to call me affectionately and say, ‘Put́uráńii, my darling, why donʼt you prepare a cháṋcii betel-leaf for me?ʼ I used to say, 'All right, father, just you wait for a minute.ʼ And my mother used to call out, 'Hey, you gatarkhági [a rural form of address used for a female labourers] miserable Puṋt́i, why donʼt you take down the pot of cooked rice off the oven? Oh, you accursed child! Look at her, she is always on the move, always working, from sunrise to sunset. And I am such a fool that I make the little girl work all the while!ʼ I used to tell her, ‘Donʼt you worry, mother. Iʼve got a human form so that I can work? Havenʼt I? Please donʼt worry about me.”

It keeps me warm in the winter and cool during the summer time.”

paragraphs.text: One meaning of the verbal root śam is “to merge oneself in some other entityʼʼ or ”to merge some other entity in oneself”. Remaining in the midst of all, one, who can gradually merge oneself in many and, in the process, imbibes the characteristics of many in oneself, is called será [the best] in Bengali.

paragraphs.text: One meaning of the word śa which we derive by adding the suffix d́a to the root śam (since Gupta era, the spelling sam has been prevalent] is also será, “the best”. One must keep in mind that será can be used only in a good or laudatory sense, and never in a derogatory sense. In other words, śa cannot be used to describe someone who is the worst among many. This word śa denotes a feminine gender.

For example, the Sun outshines all other heavenly bodies in the day sky – for this kind of objects which in Bengali is called “the best” (the greatest), the word śa will do. This word, denoting feminine gender, can be used only in a laudatory sense.

paragraphs.text: Akalmand Singh, after making great efforts, managed to become the minister of a country. His joy knew no bounds when he was made a minister. As a minister, he had no other work except to appear in ministerial meetings. The government paid for his car and house and also provided him with a monthly income. It is not that he had to work hard in the ministerial meetings, either. He mostly kept quiet, and at the end of the meeting, irrespective of his understanding of the issue at hand, he sided with the majority. He went for long drives to the east or west of the country in his official car burning up government-sponsored fuel. He would write in the logbook, “gone on urgent government work”.

You people are just wasting a poor countryʼs resources, sitting around doing nothing!”

paragraphs.text: The Minister Akalmand Singh replied, “On my way here by train, I went to the toilet. While arranging my clothes, my wallet fell down the open toilet hole. I pulled the chain, but the train didnʼt stop! I pulled it again and even hung on it – I am a heavy man weighing about five to six maunds [roughly between 189-292 kilos]. The chain broke, but even then the train didnʼt stop. To add to my midnight misery, I was then drenched by gushing water, which swelled me up and inflated me like a tom-tom. Is this a transportation system you can boast of? Is this your efficiency? Iʼll show you all… Iʼll show you all… Iʼll show you all!”

paragraphs.text: The film was actually based on a tragic story but it was full of songs and dance sequences, sound effects extravaganzas. The film was predictable, as are most musicals of its type. The hero and the heroine of the film had jumped into the sea and committed suicide. They were then cremated on a funeral pyre. The next scene showed the pair reaching hell. They exchanged garlands and were married in the presence of Yamráj [the King of Death]. Young girls ululated, the priest took his due and left; in this way the sad story ended as a comedy.

It felt even better than the time before. He sat through the night show and found the film to be better and better each time. Unfortunately, there were no more shows that day, so he reluctantly left for the hotel.

paragraphs.text: Akalmand Singh was on his way back to the hotel. To his south was the sea. But what was that bright object peeping through the tamarisk tree forest? Was it the moon or the sun? It was one oʼclock by his watch, but was it daytime or night? These two questions started troubling him, throwing his mind into a real turmoil. What was that huge blob of light in the sky? Was it one oʼclock in the afternoon or in the night? If it were indeed the moon, how could it be so large? And why would it not show itself directly and keep peeping through the tamarisk trees? Yet if it were the sun, should it not have been severely hot by now? And it had to be the moon if it was one oʼclock at night; or the sun, if it was day!

paragraphs.text: A little while ago, we were discussing about insane people and insanity. Different people act crazily regarding different matters. When things go beyond a certain point, others look at them in a curious way.

paragraphs.text: Our friend Akalmand Singh was once affected by this kind of insanity. A desire arose in his heart to be a government minister; but he did not know anything about how to become one. So he was forced to humbly approach the political chief of the area, Bhoṋdulál Singh Bed́hap, for advice. Although Bhoṋdulál was bhoṋdu [dull-witted] by name, he was not so in real life. Rather, he was quite a shrewd man. Bed́hap was his literary name. In Bengali, the word stands for “a lack of harmony” or “balance”. However the prefix be is drawn from Persian and not from Bengali.

paragraphs.text: After some days, Akalmand came to know that the Prime Minister was scheduled to visit a nearby district town. He went there in advance and waited for him.

paragraphs.text: The Prime Minister did come, but his visit was not all that peaceful. He arrived in a government plane and was there primarily for two important government projects. One, he was to inaugurate a cheap public toilet named after him and, the second, to unveil a marble bust of himself in a large park nearby. His name was Lád́d́ujilebi Singh. So the cheap toilet was named ‘Lad́d́ujilebi Cheap Toilet’. However, exactly two days before his visit, the city was thrown into turbulence by a protest about the killing of innocent people in a police firing on a violent mob in local area. Due to this the Prime Minister was not able to enter the town. He had to go back from the airport.

That would serve your purpose also. Well, let me take the first option, as that would cost you less. It costs three thousand rupees, while the second one would cost six thousand rupees. paragraphs.text: The Prime Minister had for him a few words of advice: “Since you are new to this job, I want to give you a few tips. You should never contradict the secretaries of the various departments. You should sign whatever papers they put up, on the dotted line. Instead of a signature, your left thumbimprint will do, but never use your right hand or foot. You must always pretend to know more than your secretaries; that is, at least as much as them, if not more. And as a Law Minister, read up well personal law. And, as a Labour Minister you should know that, at present, there is an unrest among the mica mines workers. The fall of market price of mica is at the root of the problem. You will have to tackle the issue carefully. Do you understand?”

footnotes.text: Caudhurii > cauddhurii > caudhurii. The word caudhurii is also prevalent in North India. Dhurii means “the hub of a wheel” in Sanskrit. Such a man is as powerful as the hub (dhura) of a wheel.

Ghat́ikál > ghad́iál > ghaŕiál > ghoŕel. A fish-eating crocodile is called a ghat́ikál. A man-eating crocodile is called a kumbhir – magarmacch in Hindi. The word has been derived from makarmatsya. In most areas of Bihar, a man-eating crocodile is called boṋchá.

chapters.title: Obtaining Leechees on a Moving Train

paragraphs.text: Speaking of tiffin (jalpán), that reminds me of a small story. It happened during British rule, when I was in my early twenties. I was taking the train from Jamalpur to Kolkata with a childhood friend, Suvimal Cakravartii (Bhońdá) and his youngest sister, Ranjana Cakravartii, alias Kheṋdi. ( 1 ) Seated next to me was a gentleman travelling from Muzaffarpur to Kolkata. Beside him was a basket filled with Muzaffarpurʼs famous leechees, that is, sháhii licus. Suvimalʼs sister, Ranjana, was a very good girl but she lacked a little common sense and had even less consideration of time, place, and person. At the time she must have been about nine.

paragraphs.text: At first, Suvimal pretended not to hear and a few minutes passed. But when “I… I… w-want… a… a… l-licu.” started again, this time with added hand and foot gestures, in other words, when she began flailing her arms and legs and saying, “I… I… w-want… a… a… l-licu.” Suvimal found himself in a predicament. He told her: “You just had a full breakfast and youʼre hungry again? Stop it. Be quiet.”

footnotes.text: In the construction of kheṋdi [snub-nosed], i is used because someone can only be kháṋdá or kheṋdi by birth. Kháṋdáʼs wife is never called kheṋdi in this sense. If she was it would be written kheṋdii. Because they are related by birth, didi [elder sister], mási [maternal aunt], pisi [paternal aunt] and similar words use i, while in-laws such as kákii [paternal uncleʼs wife] and mámii [maternal uncleʼs wife] use ii because they are not only feminine gender but feminine as well.

In Sanskrit the sound is hulu [a sound that Hindu women make during auspicious occasions]. I have heard certain pańd́its from Kerala use the word mukhavádyam also. The ancestors of Keralaʼs Náyárs came to Kerala from Ráŕh in the year 534 BCE. Thus, like Bengal, the custom of making the ulu sound is also prevalent there as well. In some Bengalee villages the practise of doing ulu is also called jokár deoyá. In ancient Bengal, people used to make this sound during auspicious functions in order to protect against anyone present who might have been thinking harmful thoughts; in other words, it was used for all auspicious undertakings.

paragraphs.text: In the waking, dream and deep-sleep states, spiritual consciousness permeates the microcosm but in the living being it happens mostly in the waking state, very little in the dream state, and virtually not at all in deep sleep. But the wonder of it is that the same being that considers the waking state the final and supreme truth, also considers the dream state as the final and supreme truth as long as he or she is dreaming. Deep sleep is the state of the experience of nothingness. Thus, despite the impossibility of calling this supreme or final, after waking from this deep sleep one falls into the error of thinking of this recent experience of absence as supreme and final. Actually, the dream state is a combination of subtle experiences collected from the mental world and vibrations collected from the waking state. Those vibrations which are gathered from the crude world oscillate constantly between truth and untruth, but those which come from the mental world are sometimes relative and sometimes non-relative truth. There is little opportunity for vibrational movement in the conviction of absence realized in deep sleep but we cannot reject this as non-existence. Anyhow, all this happens in the flow of consciousness, sometimes in a very natural, and sometimes in an unnatural rhythmic flow. This was consciousness or its negative, unconsciousness.

points.body: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, "literature"] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as 'that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = ‘with’) the trends of lifeʼ… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, 'that which co-exists with hita [welfare]ʼ. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, ‘Art for artʼs sake,ʼ cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement ‘Art for artʼs sakeʼ is not acceptable; rather we should say, 'Art for service and blessedness.ʼ… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

points.body: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted above. But he did not stop there. Going a step further, he translated his words into actions, giving a direct example by creating his own literature, which is marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories was written in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part series was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that, in October 2010, a volume named Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume was published. Now, we are extremely happy to publish Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 4, 5, 6. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all the remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

points.body: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast range of topics from linguistics and philology to history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books.

Part 5 contains eight stories from Varńa Vicitrá Part 8 which are also translated in the present volume. The last two stories (ten stories in all) are from Shabda Cayaniká Part 1, which is available in English, but properly re-edited. Part 6 contains eight long stories from Shabda Cayaniká Part 1 and 2 also properly re-edited. At the end of this note the “Sources” for each story are included.

At the beginning of each such story the author sets the scene in a way that will help the reader to understand the inner spirit of the stories.

points.body: In this respect it will be useful to quote the following: “Actually, the dream state is a combination of subtle experiences collected from the mental world and vibrations collected from the waking state. Those vibrations which are gathered from the crude world oscillate constantly between truth and untruth, but those which come from the mental world are sometimes relative and sometimes non-relative truth. There is little opportunity for vibrational movement in the conviction of absence realized in deep sleep but we cannot reject this as non-existence. Anyhow, all this happens in the flow of consciousness, sometimes in a very natural, and sometimes in an unnatural rhythmic flow. This was consciousness or its negative, unconsciousness.”

points.body: Talking about va, this reminds me of a small story. You must have seen the rows of barbers sitting by the Ganges in Baghbazar [Kolkata city]. points.body: In this context, an anecdote about ganja-addicts comes to my mind. When a newcomer joins a group of veteran ganja-addicts, he has to smoke while squatting. The novice is then called a ubu geṋjel [squatting smoker] or an ‘‘apprentice smoker’’. After gaining experience over a probationary period, he has to pass a sort of suitability or efficiency test before he is awarded a brick to sit on. When he earns the right to a brick-seat, he is no longer called a ‘squatting smoker’, but is dubbed an it́-álián-addict.

points.body: The Sanskrit root shák can also be used in the sense of “mincing something” (as in mincing vegetables) or “cutting something into pieces” (as in chipping betel-nuts). So, the word sha can be used to mean some thing that has been chopped into pieces. For example, chopped betel-nut is called sha-guváka. In ancient times, a nutcracker [yáṋti] was known as sha-yántrika (yántrika > yántia > yáṋti) [yántrika is the adjective form of yantra which means “a device or machine”]. In current Oriya, a yántrika is called guá-yántrika.

She had wonderful dexterity in making betel-leaves with just the right mix of lime and catechu. Although a trifle costly, she put some real betel-nuts in her product – a hundred percent pure betel-nuts and not the adulterated stuff of chopped coconut shells. Her conduct was excellent too. She was never ingratiating but always behaved politely. She used to bring pure betel-leaves every day all the way from Bagnan, garden-fresh so to say, because stale leaves never tasted good. Every client paid her the price she asked for, except Rámt́ahal Singh, the night watchman. Rámt́ahal Singh would casually turn up at her shop at all hours, banging the baton and demand, “Hey, Put́ii, give me a betel-leaf.” Put́uráńii would then sulkily give him one. This man never paid her, as if it were his birthright to get things for free.

Rámt́ahal takes tea over there every day but does not pay for it. The tea-vendor is too scared to ask for money. There is also a vegetable-seller nearby. Rámt́ahal often picks up potatoes and wax gourd, slices of pumpkins and other vegetables, without paying a paisa. The vegetable-seller doesnʼt have the courage to ask him to pay.

points.body: Earlier, when I had my shop in Baidyabati, I noticed the watchman there who manned the level crossing. He would stop all the vegetable-laden trucks going to the local market by lowering the barriers and take whatever he wanted of vegetables such as potatoes, bananas, etc. Then he would profit by selling the stolen vegetables at cheaper rates in the local market. Why donʼt you visit the place personally and see if I am speaking the truth or not? Donʼt announce your plans beforehand if you decide to visit the place. Go quietly, privately, because, if the sinners get to know of your plans, they will either pretend to be saints or make themselves unavailable. Your Honour, may I take your leave now ?”

points.body: “Oh yes, another matter before I go! Today you have shown everyone how to dispense justice, my son. Let the world know and learn what actual justice is all about. But I never knew how tough the job of a judge was, my son. How trying! With pen in hand, you have to sit there all day with a thoughtful expression, resting your cheek on your palms. If you work so hard, your health may give way. Do you take some milk in the morning, or do you just gulp down some tea and biscuits and come to work? Oh, what a nice boy you are, you remind me of my grandson! If he were alive today, he would be like you. Because you feel for the poor, and thus earn virtues, my son, I would like you to remain a judge for all time to come and thus – removing the suffering of the poor in this way – even in your future births. But the job of a judge is a really trying one! If you feel it is too hard for you, you could be a lawyer or a court clerk. Even in such jobs there is enough scope to do a lot of good to the poor. But if you ask me, I would like you to continue as a judge sitting on that chair for ever and ever. And I, Put́uráńii Dásii, seller of cháṋcii betel-leaves, give you my solemn word that, in every future birth of mine, I will come personally and supply you with betel-leaves. You wouldnʼt then be able to put me off, by saying that they would stain your teeth or that the spittle would be a bother! Put́uráńii wouldnʼt be swayed by such evasive arguments of yours. You would have to chew betel-leaves prepared by me whether you liked it or not!”

points.body: The Prime Minister had for him a few words of advice: “Since you are new to this job, I want to give you a few tips. You should never contradict the secretaries of the various departments. You should sign whatever papers they put up, on the dotted line. Instead of a signature, your left thumbimprint will do, but never use your right hand or foot. You must always pretend to know more than your secretaries; that is, at least as much as them, if not more. And as a Law Minister, read up well personal law. And, as a Labour Minister you should know that, at present, there is an unrest among the mica mines workers. The fall of market price of mica is at the root of the problem. You will have to tackle the issue carefully. Do you understand?”

points.body: Speaking of tiffin (jalpán), that reminds me of a small story. It happened during British rule, when I was in my early twenties. I was taking the train from Jamalpur to Kolkata with a childhood friend, Suvimal Cakravartii (Bhońdá) and his youngest sister, Ranjana Cakravartii, alias Kheṋdi. ( 1 ) Seated next to me was a gentleman travelling from Muzaffarpur to Kolkata. Beside him was a basket filled with Muzaffarpurʼs famous leechees, that is, sháhii licus. Suvimalʼs sister, Ranjana, was a very good girl but she lacked a little common sense and had even less consideration of time, place, and person. At the time she must have been about nine.

But is there anything more to the human being – does this exhaust his potential? No. The sweetness of this sense of existence is hidden in the glory of its expansion. points.body: In the waking, dream and deep-sleep states, spiritual consciousness permeates the microcosm but in the living being it happens mostly in the waking state, very little in the dream state, and virtually not at all in deep sleep. But the wonder of it is that the same being that considers the waking state the final and supreme truth, also considers the dream state as the final and supreme truth as long as he or she is dreaming. Deep sleep is the state of the experience of nothingness. Thus, despite the impossibility of calling this supreme or final, after waking from this deep sleep one falls into the error of thinking of this recent experience of absence as supreme and final. Actually, the dream state is a combination of subtle experiences collected from the mental world and vibrations collected from the waking state. Those vibrations which are gathered from the crude world oscillate constantly between truth and untruth, but those which come from the mental world are sometimes relative and sometimes non-relative truth. There is little opportunity for vibrational movement in the conviction of absence realized in deep sleep but we cannot reject this as non-existence. Anyhow, all this happens in the flow of consciousness, sometimes in a very natural, and sometimes in an unnatural rhythmic flow. This was consciousness or its negative, unconsciousness.

Doctors at that time used to wear either pants or dhoti. School boys used to wear half-pants, but as soon as they reached college age they would start wearing a dhoti and paiṋjábii.
